simpleVersion: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas did after gathering for battle at Kurukshetra.
explanation: Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe what happened after both armies gathered at Kurukshetra, the battlefield where they are about to fight.

source.sanskrit:
धृतराष्ट्र उवाच

धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः।

मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय।।1.1।।
source.transliteration:
dhṛitarāśhtra uvācha
dharma-kṣhetre kuru-kṣhetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ
māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāśhchaiva kimakurvata sañjaya
source.translation: Dhritarashtra said, "What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled together, eager for battle, on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya?"

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana sees the Pandava army arranged for battle and goes to speak with his teacher, Drona.
explanation: Sanjaya says that Duryodhana sees the Pandava army ready in formation. He then approaches Drona and begins speaking to him.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा।

आचार्यमुपसङ्गम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्।।1.2।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
dṛiṣhṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṁ vyūḍhaṁ duryodhanastadā
āchāryamupasaṅgamya rājā vachanamabravīt
source.translation: Sanjaya said: Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher, Drona, and spoke these words.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

hook: What would it feel like to face an army organized by someone you once taught?
simpleVersion: Duryodhana points out the large Pandava army to Drona and notes that Dhrishtadyumna, Drona’s student, arranged it.
explanation: Duryodhana tells Drona to look at the powerful Pandava army. He points out that it was arranged by Dhrishtadyumna, the son of Drupada and one of Drona’s students.

source.sanskrit:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम्।

व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता।।1.3।।
source.transliteration:
paśhyaitāṁ pāṇḍu-putrāṇām āchārya mahatīṁ chamūm
vyūḍhāṁ drupada-putreṇa tava śhiṣhyeṇa dhīmatā
source.translation: Behold, O Teacher! This mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: The Pandava army includes powerful archers and warriors such as Yuyudhana, Virata, and Drupada.
explanation: Duryodhana names several strong warriors on the Pandava side. He describes them as mighty fighters, comparing their battlefield strength with Bhima and Arjuna.

source.sanskrit:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि।

युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः।।1.4।।
source.transliteration:
atra śhūrā maheṣhvāsā bhīmārjuna-samā yudhi
yuyudhāno virāṭaśhcha drupadaśhcha mahā-rathaḥ
source.translation: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yuyudhana (Satyaki), Virata, and Drupada—all mighty warriors.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: More powerful kings and warriors are named, including Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the king of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya.
explanation: Duryodhana continues listing notable warriors on the Pandava side. He names several kings and fighters and describes them as outstanding men.

source.sanskrit:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान्।

पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुङ्गवः।।1.5।।
source.transliteration:
dhṛiṣhṭaketuśhchekitānaḥ kāśhirājaśhcha vīryavān
purujit kuntibhojaśhcha śhaibyaśhcha nara-puṅgavaḥ
yudhāmanyuśhcha vikrānta uttamaujāśhcha vīryavān
source.translation: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya—the best of men.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: The list continues with Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, and the sons of Draupadi, all described as great warriors.
explanation: Duryodhana names more major fighters on the Pandava side: Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, and Draupadi’s sons. He describes all of them as great chariot warriors.

source.sanskrit:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान्।

सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः।।1.6।।
source.transliteration: saubhadro draupadeyāśhcha sarva eva mahā-rathāḥ
source.translation: The strong Yudhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of Draupadi, all of them great charioteers (great heroes)."

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana now turns to the important commanders on his own side and begins naming them for Drona.
explanation: After describing the opposing army, Duryodhana says he will identify the important leaders of his own army so Drona knows who they are.

source.sanskrit:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम।

नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते।।1.7।।
source.transliteration:
asmākaṁ tu viśhiṣhṭā ye tānnibodha dwijottama
nāyakā mama sainyasya sanjñārthaṁ tānbravīmi te
source.translation: Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to you for your information.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana names Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava as powerful warriors ready for battle.
explanation: Duryodhana lists several major fighters on his side, including Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Ashvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava, and describes them as ready for battle.

source.sanskrit:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिञ्जयः।

अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च।।1.8।।
source.transliteration:
bhavānbhīṣhmaśhcha karṇaśhcha kṛipaśhcha samitiñjayaḥ
aśhvatthāmā vikarṇaśhcha saumadattis tathaiva cha
source.translation: "Thou thyself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta—all these are ready for battle."

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: Many other skilled warriors are also ready to fight and are willing to risk their lives for Duryodhana’s side.
explanation: Duryodhana says that many other brave and highly skilled warriors are armed with different weapons and are prepared to give their lives in the battle.

source.sanskrit:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः।

नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः।।1.9।।
source.transliteration:
anye cha bahavaḥ śhūrā madarthe tyaktajīvitāḥ
nānā-śhastra-praharaṇāḥ sarve yuddha-viśhāradāḥ
source.translation: And also many other heroes, ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled in battle.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana says that his army protected by Bhishma is insufficient, while he considers the Pandava army protected by Bhima sufficient.
explanation: Duryodhana compares the two armies. According to the supplied translation, he calls his own force insufficient even though Bhishma protects it, while he calls the Pandava force sufficient under Bhima’s protection.

source.sanskrit:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम्।

पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम्।।1.10।।
source.transliteration:
aparyāptaṁ tadasmākaṁ balaṁ bhīṣhmābhirakṣhitam
paryāptaṁ tvidameteṣhāṁ balaṁ bhīmābhirakṣhitam
source.translation: Our army, marshalled by Bhishma, is insufficient, whereas theirs, marshalled by Bhima, is sufficient.

editorialReview: Chapter 1 editorial pass v1: simplified for clarity, removed unsupported interpretation, hooks only when genuinely supported.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana tells every warrior to stay in position and protect Bhishma above all.
explanation: Duryodhana instructs his soldiers to remain at their assigned positions and make protecting Bhishma their main priority.

source.sanskrit:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः।

भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि।।1.11।।
source.transliteration:
ayaneṣhu cha sarveṣhu yathā-bhāgamavasthitāḥ
bhīṣhmamevābhirakṣhantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi
source.translation: Therefore, do all of you, stationed in your respective positions in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone.

simpleVersion: Bhishma roars like a lion and blows his conch to cheer Duryodhana.
explanation: Bhishma, the eldest of the Kauravas, gives a powerful roar and blows his conch to encourage Duryodhana before the battle begins.

source.sanskrit:
तस्य संजनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः।

सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान्।।1.12।।
source.transliteration:
tasya sañjanayan harṣhaṁ kuru-vṛiddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ
siṁha-nādaṁ vinadyochchaiḥ śhaṅkhaṁ dadhmau pratāpavān
source.translation: His glorious grandsire, the oldest of the Kauravas, roared like a lion to cheer Duryodhana and blew his conch.

simpleVersion: Conches, drums, and horns suddenly sound together, creating a tremendous noise from the Kaurava side.
explanation: After Bhishma sounds his conch, many instruments across the Kaurava army begin to play. Their combined sound fills the battlefield.

source.sanskrit:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः।

सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत्।।1.13।।
source.transliteration:
tataḥ śhaṅkhāśhcha bheryaśhcha paṇavānaka-gomukhāḥ
sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śhabdastumulo ’bhavat
source.translation: Then, suddenly, conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and cow horns blared forth from the Kaurava side, and the sound was tremendous.

simpleVersion: Krishna and Arjuna answer by blowing their divine conches from their magnificent chariot drawn by white horses.
explanation: Krishna and Arjuna are seated together in a great chariot pulled by white horses. They respond by sounding their own conches.

source.sanskrit:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ।

माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः।।1.14।।
source.transliteration:
tataḥ śhvetairhayairyukte mahati syandane sthitau
mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaśhchaiva divyau śhaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ
source.translation: Then, Madhava (Krishna) and the son of Pandu (Arjuna), seated in the magnificent chariot yoked with white horses, blew divine conches.

simpleVersion: Krishna, Arjuna, and Bhima each blow their own famous conches: Panchajanya, Devadatta, and Paundra.
explanation: The verse names the three conches sounded by Krishna, Arjuna, and Bhima. Each warrior has a different conch with its own name.

source.sanskrit:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनंजयः।

पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः।।1.15।।
source.transliteration:
pāñchajanyaṁ hṛiṣhīkeśho devadattaṁ dhanañjayaḥ
pauṇḍraṁ dadhmau mahā-śhaṅkhaṁ bhīma-karmā vṛikodaraḥ
source.translation: Hrishikesha blew the Panchajanya, Arjuna blew the Devadatta, and Bhima, the wolf-bellied doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.

simpleVersion: Yudhishthira, Nakula, and Sahadeva also sound their conches, each using a conch with its own name.
explanation: Yudhishthira blows the Anantavijaya, while Nakula and Sahadeva blow the Sughosha and Manipushpaka.

source.sanskrit:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः।

नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ।।1.16।।
source.transliteration:
anantavijayaṁ rājā kuntī-putro yudhiṣhṭhiraḥ
nakulaḥ sahadevaśhcha sughoṣha-maṇipuṣhpakau
source.translation: King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka.

simpleVersion: Several other Pandava warriors, including the king of Kasi, Sikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Satyaki, sound their conches.
explanation: The verse continues naming important warriors on the Pandava side who join the call by blowing their conches.

source.sanskrit:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः।

धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः।।1.17।।
source.transliteration:
kāśhyaśhcha parameṣhvāsaḥ śhikhaṇḍī cha mahā-rathaḥ
dhṛiṣhṭadyumno virāṭaśhcha sātyakiśh chāparājitaḥ
source.translation: The king of Kasi, an excellent archer, Sikhandi, the mighty car-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Satyaki, the unconquered.

simpleVersion: Drupada, Draupadi's sons, and Abhimanyu also blow their conches, each sounding his own.
explanation: Drupada, the sons of Draupadi, and Abhimanyu each sound their own conches as the Pandava warriors prepare for battle.

source.sanskrit:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते।

सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक्।।1.18।।
source.transliteration:
drupado draupadeyāśhcha sarvaśhaḥ pṛithivī-pate
saubhadraśhcha mahā-bāhuḥ śhaṅkhāndadhmuḥ pṛithak pṛithak
source.translation: Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, O Lord of the Earth, and the son of Subhadra, the mighty-armed, blew their conches each separately.

simpleVersion: The combined sound of the Pandava conches shakes the hearts of Dhritarashtra's warriors and echoes through heaven and earth.
explanation: The many conches create a huge, powerful sound. The verse says this sound deeply affects the warriors on Dhritarashtra's side.

source.sanskrit:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत्।

नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलो व्यनुनादयन्।।1.19।।
source.transliteration:
sa ghoṣho dhārtarāṣhṭrāṇāṁ hṛidayāni vyadārayat
nabhaśhcha pṛithivīṁ chaiva tumulo nunādayan
source.translation: The tumultuous sound rent the hearts of Dhritarashtra's party, reverberating through both heaven and earth.

hook: Just before the first weapons clash, Arjuna stops to speak.
simpleVersion: Just before the weapons are about to clash, Arjuna raises his bow and turns to speak to Krishna.
explanation: Arjuna sees Dhritarashtra's warriors standing ready for battle. As the fighting is about to begin, he takes up his bow and speaks to Krishna.

source.sanskrit:
अथ व्यवस्थितान् दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान्कपिध्वजः।

प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसंपाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः।।1.20।।
source.transliteration:
atha vyavasthitān dṛiṣhṭvā dhārtarāṣhṭrān kapi-dhwajaḥ
pravṛitte śhastra-sampāte dhanurudyamya pāṇḍavaḥ
source.translation: Then, seeing the people of Dhritarashtra's party standing arrayed and the discharge of weapons about to begin, Arjuna, the son of Pandu whose ensign was a monkey, took up his bow and said the following to Krishna, O Lord of the Earth.

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks Krishna to place his chariot between the two armies.
explanation: Arjuna asks Krishna to move their chariot into the space between the two sides. He wants to look closely at the people gathered for the battle.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

हृषीकेशं तदा वाक्यमिदमाह महीपते।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत।।1.21।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
senayor ubhayor madhye rathaṁ sthāpaya me ’chyuta
source.translation: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, place my chariot in the middle between the two armies."

hook: Who exactly am I about to fight?
simpleVersion: Arjuna wants to see the warriors he is expected to fight before the battle begins.
explanation: Arjuna wants to look at the people standing ready to fight. He wants to know exactly who he will be facing when the battle starts.

source.sanskrit:
यावदेतान्निरीक्षेऽहं योद्धुकामानवस्थितान्।

कैर्मया सह योद्धव्यमस्मिन्रणसमुद्यमे।।1.22।।
source.transliteration:
yāvadetān nirīkṣhe ’haṁ yoddhu-kāmān avasthitān
kairmayā saha yoddhavyam asmin raṇa-samudyame
source.translation: ...so that I may behold those who stand here, desirous to fight, and know with whom I must fight when the battle is about to commence.

simpleVersion: Arjuna wants to see the warriors who have gathered to fight for Duryodhana.
explanation: Arjuna explains that he wants to look at the people who have assembled to fight on Duryodhana's side. He describes Duryodhana as evil-minded.

source.sanskrit:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः।

धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः।।1.23।।
source.transliteration:
yotsyamānān avekṣhe ’haṁ ya ete ’tra samāgatāḥ
dhārtarāṣhṭrasya durbuddher yuddhe priya-chikīrṣhavaḥ
source.translation: For I desire to observe those who are assembled here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded Duryodhana—the son of Dhritarashtra.

simpleVersion: Krishna moves their chariot between the two armies, just as Arjuna asked.
explanation: Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Krishna follows Arjuna's request and places their chariot in the middle of the two armies.

source.sanskrit:
संजय उवाच

एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम्।।1.24।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam ukto hṛiṣhīkeśho guḍākeśhena bhārata
senayor ubhayor madhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam
source.translation: Sanjaya said, Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna stationed the best of chariots, O Dhritarashtra, in the midst of the two armies.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to look at the Kurus gathered for battle.
explanation: Krishna places the chariot before Bhishma, Drona, and the other rulers. He then tells Arjuna to look at the Kurus gathered there.

source.sanskrit:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम्।

उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति।।1.25।।
source.transliteration:
bhīṣhma-droṇa-pramukhataḥ sarveṣhāṁ cha mahī-kṣhitām
uvācha pārtha paśhyaitān samavetān kurūn iti
source.translation: In front of Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, he said: "O Arjuna, son of Pritha, behold these Kurus gathered together."

hook: The battlefield is full of people Arjuna knows.
simpleVersion: Arjuna sees teachers, relatives, friends, and several generations of his family standing in both armies.
explanation: Arjuna looks across the battlefield and recognizes people he knows: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends. They are standing on both sides.

source.sanskrit:
तत्रापश्यत्स्थितान्पार्थः पितृ़नथ पितामहान्।

आचार्यान्मातुलान्भ्रातृ़न्पुत्रान्पौत्रान्सखींस्तथा।।1.26।।
source.transliteration:
tatrāpaśhyat sthitān pārthaḥ pitṝīn atha pitāmahān
āchāryān mātulān bhrātṝīn putrān pautrān sakhīṁs tathā
source.translation: Then, Arjuna (son of Pritha) saw there (in the armies) stationed fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.

simpleVersion: Arjuna also sees fathers-in-law and friends among the warriors on both sides.
explanation: Arjuna continues looking at the two armies. He sees even more close relatives, including fathers-in-law and friends, standing ready for battle.

source.sanskrit:
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि।

तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान्।।1.27।।
source.transliteration: tān samīkṣhya sa kaunteyaḥ sarvān bandhūn avasthitān
source.translation: He saw fathers-in-law and friends in both the armies. The son of Kunti, Arjuna, seeing all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed.

hook: What happens when the people you must fight are your own family?
simpleVersion: Seeing his own family ready to fight, Arjuna becomes overwhelmed with sorrow.
explanation: Arjuna sees his relatives gathered and ready to fight. The sight fills him with deep pity and sorrow, and he begins speaking to Krishna about what he is feeling.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

कृपया परयाऽऽविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत्।

दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम्।।1.28।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
kṛipayā parayāviṣhṭo viṣhīdann idam abravīt
dṛiṣhṭvemaṁ sva-janaṁ kṛiṣhṇa yuyutsuṁ samupasthitam
source.translation: Arjuna, overcome with deep pity, sorrowing, said: "O Krishna, seeing my kinsmen arrayed here, eager to fight,

simpleVersion: Arjuna's distress becomes physical: his limbs weaken, his mouth dries, and his body starts trembling.
explanation: Arjuna describes what is happening to his body. His limbs feel weak, his mouth becomes dry, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end.

source.sanskrit:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति।

वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते।।1.29।।
source.transliteration:
sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṁ cha pariśhuṣhyati
vepathuśh cha śharīre me roma-harṣhaśh cha jāyate
source.translation: My limbs fail, my mouth is parched, my body quivers, and my hair stands on end.

simpleVersion: Arjuna's distress grows stronger: his bow slips, his skin burns, he cannot stand, and his mind feels confused.
explanation: Arjuna says he can no longer hold his bow properly. His skin feels as if it is burning, he cannot stand steadily, and his mind feels as though it is reeling.

source.sanskrit:
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते।

न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः।।1.30।।
source.transliteration:
gāṇḍīvaṁ sraṁsate hastāt tvak chaiva paridahyate
na cha śhaknomy avasthātuṁ bhramatīva cha me manaḥ
source.translation: The Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns all over; I am unable to stand, and my mind is reeling, as it were.

simpleVersion: Arjuna sees bad omens and says he can see no good in killing his own relatives.
explanation: Arjuna says he sees signs of trouble and cannot see any good outcome in killing his own family members in battle.

source.sanskrit:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव।

न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे।।1.31।।
source.transliteration:
nimittāni cha paśhyāmi viparītāni keśhava
na cha śhreyo ’nupaśhyāmi hatvā sva-janam āhave
source.translation: And I see ill omens, O Kesava. I do not see any good in slaying my kinsmen in battle.

hook: What is victory worth if the people you would share it with are the ones you must fight?
simpleVersion: Arjuna says he no longer wants victory, a kingdom, or pleasure if getting them means killing his own people.
explanation: Arjuna says the usual rewards of war—victory, a kingdom, and enjoyment—have lost their value because the people connected to those rewards are standing before him as opponents.

source.sanskrit:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च।

किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा।।1.32।।
source.transliteration:
na kāṅkṣhe vijayaṁ kṛiṣhṇa na cha rājyaṁ sukhāni cha
kiṁ no rājyena govinda kiṁ bhogair jīvitena vā
source.translation:
I desire not victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
What use is dominion to us, O Krishna, or pleasures or even life?

simpleVersion: The very people Arjuna would want to enjoy the kingdom with are now standing on the battlefield against him.
explanation: Arjuna points out that the relatives whose sake he would want a kingdom and its pleasures are now risking their lives in the war.

source.sanskrit:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च।

त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च।।1.33।।
source.transliteration:
yeṣhām arthe kāṅkṣhitaṁ no rājyaṁ bhogāḥ sukhāni cha
ta ime ’vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṁs tyaktvā dhanāni cha
source.translation: Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures stand here in battle, having renounced life and wealth.

simpleVersion: Arjuna sees teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles, in-laws, grandsons, and other relatives on the opposing side.
explanation: Arjuna continues naming the many kinds of family members and close relatives standing in the armies before him.

source.sanskrit:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः।

मातुलाः श्चशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः सम्बन्धिनस्तथा।।1.34।।
source.transliteration:
āchāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrās tathaiva cha pitāmahāḥ
mātulāḥ śhvaśhurāḥ pautrāḥ śhyālāḥ sambandhinas tathā
source.translation: Teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—

hook: Some things are not worth gaining at any cost.
simpleVersion: Arjuna refuses to kill these relatives even if it means giving up his life, let alone for the sake of a kingdom.
explanation: Arjuna says he does not want to kill these people even if they attack him. He would not do so even for control of the three worlds, much less for an earthly kingdom.

source.sanskrit:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन।

अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते।।1.35।।
source.transliteration:
etān na hantum ichchhāmi ghnato ’pi madhusūdana
api trailokya-rājyasya hetoḥ kiṁ nu mahī-kṛite
source.translation: These I do not wish to kill, O Krishna, even though they kill me, for the sake of dominion over the three worlds; leave alone killing them for the sake of the earth."

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks what happiness could come from killing Dhritarashtra's sons, whom he considers aggressors.
explanation: Arjuna questions whether killing the opposing side could bring happiness. He says that killing these aggressors would instead bring sin.

source.sanskrit:
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन।

पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः।।1.36।।
source.transliteration:
nihatya dhārtarāṣhṭrān naḥ kā prītiḥ syāj janārdana
pāpam evāśhrayed asmān hatvaitān ātatāyinaḥ
source.translation: By killing these sons of Dhritarashtra, what pleasure could be ours, O Janardana? Only sin would accrue to us from killing these felons.

simpleVersion: Arjuna argues that they should not kill their own relatives because he cannot see how killing them could bring happiness.
explanation: Arjuna concludes that killing their relatives is wrong in his view. He asks how they could expect to be happy after killing their own family.

source.sanskrit:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान्।

स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव।।1.37।।
source.transliteration:
tasmān nārhā vayaṁ hantuṁ dhārtarāṣhṭrān sa-bāndhavān 
sva-janaṁ hi kathaṁ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava
source.translation: Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own kin, O Madhava (Krishna)?

simpleVersion: Arjuna says that greed may prevent the other side from seeing the harm of destroying families and turning against friends.
explanation: Arjuna says the opposing side, whose judgment he sees as affected by greed, does not recognize the wrongdoing he believes would come from destroying families and betraying friends.

source.sanskrit:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः।

कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम्।।1.38।।
source.transliteration:
yady apy ete na paśhyanti lobhopahata-chetasaḥ
kula-kṣhaya-kṛitaṁ doṣhaṁ mitra-drohe cha pātakam
source.translation: Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of families and no sin in hostility to friends,

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks why they should commit the same wrong when they already understand the harm he sees in destroying a family.
explanation: Arjuna argues that because they understand what he considers wrong about destroying families and harming friends, they should not knowingly commit those acts.

source.sanskrit:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम्।

कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन।।1.39।।
source.transliteration:
kathaṁ na jñeyam asmābhiḥ pāpād asmān nivartitum
kula-kṣhaya-kṛitaṁ doṣhaṁ prapaśhyadbhir janārdana
source.translation: Why should we not, who clearly see the evil in the destruction of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)?

simpleVersion: Arjuna says that when a family is destroyed, its long-standing traditions and duties can also disappear.
explanation: Arjuna argues that destroying a family also damages the traditions and duties passed down through generations. He says disorder then takes their place.

source.sanskrit:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः।

धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत।।1.40।।
source.transliteration:
kula-kṣhaye praṇaśhyanti kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ
dharme naṣhṭe kulaṁ kṛitsnam adharmo ’bhibhavaty uta
source.translation: In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety indeed, overwhelms the whole family.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says that when family duties break down, disorder spreads through the family and its social structure.
explanation: Continuing his argument, Arjuna says that when family traditions and duties are lost, the resulting disorder affects the wider family structure.

source.sanskrit:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः।

स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसङ्करः।।1.41।।
source.transliteration:
adharmābhibhavāt kṛiṣhṇa praduṣhyanti kula-striyaḥ
strīṣhu duṣhṭāsu vārṣhṇeya jāyate varṇa-saṅkaraḥ
source.translation: O Krishna, by the prevalence of impiety, the women of the family become corrupt; and, when women are corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), intermingling of castes arises.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says this disorder also harms the family's ancestors because traditional offerings and rites would no longer be properly maintained.
explanation: Arjuna continues his argument by saying that when family duties disappear, the traditional rites performed for ancestors are also lost.

source.sanskrit:
सङ्करो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च।

पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः।।1.42।।
source.transliteration:
saṅkaro narakāyaiva kula-ghnānāṁ kulasya cha
patanti pitaro hy eṣhāṁ lupta-piṇḍodaka-kriyāḥ
source.translation: Confusion of castes leads to hell for the slayers of the family, for their forebears fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and libations of water.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says that these wrong actions ultimately destroy the family's long-standing duties and traditions.
explanation: Arjuna concludes this part of his argument by saying that the consequences he has described lead to the destruction of the family's established duties and traditions.

source.sanskrit:
दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसङ्करकारकैः।

उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः।।1.43।।
source.transliteration:
doṣhair etaiḥ kula-ghnānāṁ varṇa-saṅkara-kārakaiḥ
utsādyante jāti-dharmāḥ kula-dharmāśh cha śhāśhvatāḥ
source.translation: By these evil deeds of the destroyers of the family, which cause confusion of castes, the eternal religious rites of the caste and the family are destroyed.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he has heard that people from families whose duties are destroyed suffer serious consequences after death.
explanation: Arjuna refers to a teaching he has heard: when a family's traditional duties are destroyed, those affected are believed to suffer for a long time.

source.sanskrit:
उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन।

नरकेऽनियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम।।1.44।।
source.transliteration:
utsanna-kula-dharmāṇāṁ manuṣhyāṇāṁ janārdana
narake ‘niyataṁ vāso bhavatītyanuśhuśhruma
source.translation: We have heard, O Janardana, that those men in whose families the religious practices have been destroyed are inevitably destined to dwell in hell for an unknown period.

hook: What if the prize you want is not worth the harm it takes to obtain it?
simpleVersion: Arjuna laments that they are about to commit a terrible wrong because of their desire for the pleasures of a kingdom.
explanation: Arjuna says they are about to commit what he considers a great sin, driven by the desire for royal pleasures and power, even though their own relatives stand before them.

source.sanskrit:
अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम्।

यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः।।1.45।।
source.transliteration:
aho bata mahat pāpaṁ kartuṁ vyavasitā vayam
yad rājya-sukha-lobhena hantuṁ sva-janam udyatāḥ
source.translation: Alas! We are involved in a great sin, for we are prepared to kill our kinsmen, out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he would rather be killed without fighting than kill his own relatives in this war.
explanation: Arjuna declares that he would prefer to die unarmed and without resisting rather than fight and kill the armed sons of Dhritarashtra.

source.sanskrit:
यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः।

धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत्।।1.46।।
source.transliteration:
yadi mām apratīkāram aśhastraṁ śhastra-pāṇayaḥ
dhārtarāṣhṭrā raṇe hanyus tan me kṣhemataraṁ bhavet
source.translation: If the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya says Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sits down in his chariot, overwhelmed by grief.
explanation: After expressing his anguish, Arjuna puts down his weapons and sits in his chariot, overcome with sorrow.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

एवमुक्त्वाऽर्जुनः संख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत्।

विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः।।1.47।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam uktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśhat
visṛijya sa-śharaṁ chāpaṁ śhoka-saṁvigna-mānasaḥ
source.translation: Sanjaya said, Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna cast away his bow and arrow and, his mind overwhelmed with sorrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya says Krishna begins speaking to Arjuna, who is sitting overwhelmed by pity, sorrow, and tears.
explanation: Arjuna is still overcome by grief when Krishna begins to speak to him. This verse simply sets the emotional scene for Krishna's teaching.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

तं तथा कृपयाऽविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम्।

विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः।।2.1।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
taṁ tathā kṛipayāviṣhṭamaśhru pūrṇākulekṣhaṇam
viṣhīdantamidaṁ vākyam uvācha madhusūdanaḥ
source.translation: Sanjaya said: To him, who was thus overcome with pity, despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.

hook: When fear and confusion take over, what makes you step back into your purpose?
simpleVersion: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair and asks why he has fallen into a state he considers unworthy of him.
explanation: Krishna directly questions Arjuna's sudden despair and tells him that this weakness does not suit him. He urges Arjuna to rise above it.

source.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम्।

अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन।।2.2।।
source.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
kutastvā kaśhmalamidaṁ viṣhame samupasthitam
anārya-juṣhṭamaswargyam akīrti-karam arjuna
source.translation: The Blessed Lord said, "From whence has this perilous strait come upon you, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon you, O Arjuna?"

hook: Stand up when weakness tells you to give up.
simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to reject his weakness and rise to face the battle.
explanation: Krishna firmly tells Arjuna to cast aside what He calls weakness of heart and stand up. The verse is a direct call to regain courage and act.

source.sanskrit:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते।

क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप।।2.3।।
source.transliteration:
klaibyaṁ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitat tvayyupapadyate
kṣhudraṁ hṛidaya-daurbalyaṁ tyaktvottiṣhṭha parantapa
source.translation: Do not yield to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit you. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O conqueror of foes!

hook: How do you fight when the people before you are the teachers you revere?
simpleVersion: Arjuna asks how he can fight Bhishma and Drona, two elders he deeply respects.
explanation: Arjuna cannot understand how he is supposed to shoot at Bhishma and Drona when he regards both as worthy of honor.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

कथं भीष्ममहं संख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन।

इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन।।2.4।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
kathaṁ bhīṣhmam ahaṁ sankhye droṇaṁ cha madhusūdana
iṣhubhiḥ pratiyotsyāmi pūjārhāvari-sūdana
source.translation: Arjuna said, "O Madhusudana, how can I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of being worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?"

simpleVersion: Arjuna would rather live by begging than kill his respected teachers and enjoy wealth gained through their deaths.
explanation: Arjuna says that living on alms would be better than killing his noble teachers. Any wealth or pleasure gained from killing them would feel stained by their blood.

source.sanskrit:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्

श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके।

हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव

भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान्।।2.5।।
source.transliteration:
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān
śhreyo bhoktuṁ bhaikṣhyamapīha loke
hatvārtha-kāmāṁstu gurūnihaiva
bhuñjīya bhogān rudhira-pradigdhān
source.translation: Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I were to kill them, even in this world, all my enjoyments of wealth and fulfilled desires would be stained with their blood.

hook: What if you cannot tell whether winning or losing is the worse choice?
simpleVersion: Arjuna admits he cannot decide whether victory or defeat would be better because the people he would have to kill are standing before him.
explanation: Arjuna is deeply conflicted. He cannot see which outcome is preferable when either victory or defeat involves people he does not want to kill.

source.sanskrit:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो

यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः।

यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषाम

स्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः।।2.6।।
source.transliteration:
na chaitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo
yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ
yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣhāmas
te ’vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣhṭrāḥ
source.translation: I can hardly tell which would be better, that we should conquer them or that they should conquer us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, whom we do not wish to slay, stand facing us.

hook: Sometimes the wisest thing you can say is: I don't know—teach me.
simpleVersion: Arjuna admits he is confused about his duty and asks Krishna to clearly tell him what is right.
explanation: Arjuna stops trying to solve the conflict alone. He accepts Krishna as his teacher and asks for a definite path that will lead to his highest good.

source.sanskrit:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः

पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः।

यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्िचतं ब्रूहि तन्मे

शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम्।।2.7।।
source.transliteration:
kārpaṇya-doṣhopahata-svabhāvaḥ
pṛichchhāmi tvāṁ dharma-sammūḍha-chetāḥ
yach-chhreyaḥ syānniśhchitaṁ brūhi tanme
śhiṣhyaste ’haṁ śhādhi māṁ tvāṁ prapannam
source.translation: My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to my duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple; instruct me, who has taken refuge in Thee.

hook: What could be worth having if it cannot remove your deepest grief?
simpleVersion: Arjuna says that not even unrivaled power on earth or heaven could remove the sorrow consuming him.
explanation: Arjuna says his grief is so deep that even immense worldly power or heavenly authority would not remove it.

source.sanskrit:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्या

द्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम्।

अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्

राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्।।2.8।।
source.transliteration:
na hi prapaśhyāmi mamāpanudyād
yach-chhokam uchchhoṣhaṇam-indriyāṇām
avāpya bhūmāv-asapatnamṛiddhaṁ
rājyaṁ surāṇāmapi chādhipatyam
source.translation: I do not see that this sorrow that burns up my senses would be removed, even if I were to attain prosperous and unrivaled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he will not fight, then becomes silent.
explanation: After explaining his doubts, Arjuna tells Krishna that he will not fight and then falls silent.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप।

न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह।।2.9।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam-uktvā hṛiṣhīkeśhaṁ guḍākeśhaḥ parantapa
na yotsya iti govindam uktvā tūṣhṇīṁ babhūva ha
source.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, the Lord of the senses, Arjuna, the conqueror of sleep and destroyer of foes, said, "I will not fight," and became silent.

hook: Even in the middle of despair, Krishna remains calm.
simpleVersion: Sanjaya says Krishna, smiling, begins speaking to the despondent Arjuna between the two armies.
explanation: Arjuna is still overwhelmed, but Krishna responds with a smile and begins His teaching. The verse introduces the transition from Arjuna's despair to Krishna's instruction.

source.sanskrit:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः।।2.10।।
source.transliteration:
tam-uvācha hṛiṣhīkeśhaḥ prahasanniva bhārata
senayorubhayor-madhye viṣhīdantam-idaṁ vachaḥ
source.translation: To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words.

hook: Not every thought that sounds wise is true wisdom.
simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna that his grief is misplaced, despite the wise-sounding words he has been speaking.
explanation: Krishna begins correcting Arjuna's reasoning. He says that the truly wise do not grieve for the living or the dead in the way Arjuna is doing.

source.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे।

गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः।।2.11।।
source.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
aśhochyān-anvaśhochas-tvaṁ prajñā-vādānśh cha bhāṣhase
gatāsūn-agatāsūnśh-cha nānuśhochanti paṇḍitāḥ
source.translation: The Blessed Lord said, "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for; yet, you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead."

hook: What if death changes the body, but not the deepest self?
simpleVersion: Krishna says that He, Arjuna, and these kings have always existed and will continue to exist.
explanation: Krishna teaches that the individual self does not simply begin with this life or end with death. He says that He, Arjuna, and the others have existed before and will continue to exist.

source.sanskrit:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः।

न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम्।।2.12।।
source.transliteration:
na tvevāhaṁ jātu nāsaṁ na tvaṁ neme janādhipāḥ
na chaiva na bhaviṣhyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param
source.translation: Nor, at any time, was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men; nor, verily, shall we ever cease to be hereafter.

hook: The body changes from childhood to old age—Krishna says death is another change of body.
simpleVersion: Krishna compares death to the body's earlier changes from childhood to youth and old age, saying the embodied self continues into another body.
explanation: The verse uses the familiar changes of a human lifetime to explain Krishna's teaching that the embodied self continues beyond the present body.

source.sanskrit:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा।

तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति।।2.13।।
source.transliteration:
dehino ’smin yathā dehe kaumāraṁ yauvanaṁ jarā
tathā dehāntara-prāptir dhīras tatra na muhyati
source.translation: Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it pass into another body; the steadfast one does not grieve over this.

simpleVersion: Heat, cold, pleasure, and pain come and go, so Krishna tells Arjuna to endure these temporary experiences steadily.
explanation: Krishna says sensory experiences have a beginning and an end. Because they are temporary, He tells Arjuna to remain steady while experiencing them.

source.sanskrit:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः।

आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत।।2.14।।
source.transliteration:
mātrā-sparśhās tu kaunteya śhītoṣhṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ
āgamāpāyino ’nityās tans-titikṣhasva bhārata
source.translation: The contact of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which causes heat and cold, pleasure and pain, has a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them bravely, O Arjuna.

simpleVersion: A person who stays steady through pleasure and pain becomes fit for the state Krishna calls immortality.
explanation: Krishna praises the person who remains balanced through pleasure and pain. Such steadiness is described as a qualification for attaining immortality.

source.sanskrit:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ।

समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते।।2.15।।
source.transliteration:
yaṁ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣhaṁ puruṣharṣhabha
sama-duḥkha-sukhaṁ dhīraṁ so ’mṛitatvāya kalpate
source.translation: That firm man, whom surely these afflictions do not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality.

hook: Some things pass away; Krishna says the real does not.
simpleVersion: Krishna distinguishes between what is temporary and what is truly real, saying the real does not cease to exist.
explanation: Krishna says the unreal has no lasting existence, while the real does not cease to be. Those who see truth understand this distinction.

source.sanskrit:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः।

उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः।।2.16।।
source.transliteration:
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ
ubhayorapi dṛiṣhṭo ’nta stvanayos tattva-darśhibhiḥ
source.translation: The unreal has no being; there is no non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the truth (or the seers of the essence).

simpleVersion: Krishna says the Self that pervades everything is indestructible and cannot be destroyed.
explanation: Krishna describes the underlying Self as imperishable. Nothing can bring about its destruction.

source.sanskrit:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम्।

विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित् कर्तुमर्हति।।2.17।।
source.transliteration:
avināśhi tu tadviddhi yena sarvam idaṁ tatam
vināśham avyayasyāsya na kaśhchit kartum arhati
source.translation: Know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded. No one can cause the destruction of that, the Imperishable.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the Self is unmanifest, beyond ordinary thought, and unchanging, so Arjuna should not grieve on that account.
explanation: Krishna describes the Self as beyond ordinary perception and thought and tells Arjuna that, knowing this, he should not grieve.

source.sanskrit:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः।

अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत।।2.18।।
source.transliteration:
antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śharīriṇaḥ
anāśhino ’prameyasya tasmād yudhyasva bhārata
source.translation: These bodies of the embodied Self, which are eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore, fight, O Arjuna.

simpleVersion: Even if Arjuna believed life and death happen repeatedly, Krishna says he still should not grieve.
explanation: Krishna temporarily sets aside the previous argument and considers another view: even if the self were thought to be repeatedly born and dying, He says grief would still not be appropriate.

source.sanskrit:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम्।

उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते।।2.19।।
source.transliteration:
ya enaṁ vetti hantāraṁ yaśh chainaṁ manyate hatam
ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṁ hanti na hanyate
source.translation: He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks it is slain, neither of them knows. It does not slay, nor is it slain.

hook: Death is certain for the born; Krishna asks Arjuna not to grieve over what cannot be avoided.
simpleVersion: Krishna says death follows birth and birth follows death, so Arjuna should not grieve over the inevitable.
explanation: Krishna presents birth and death as an unavoidable cycle. Because the event cannot be prevented, He tells Arjuna not to grieve over it.

source.sanskrit:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचि

न्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः।

अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो

न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे।।2.20।।
source.transliteration:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadāchin
nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ
ajo nityaḥ śhāśhvato ’yaṁ purāṇo
na hanyate hanyamāne śharīre
source.translation: It is not born, nor does it ever die; after having been, it again does not cease to be; unborn, eternal, changeless, and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.

simpleVersion: Krishna says beings are unseen before birth, visible during life, and unseen again after death, then asks what there is to grieve.
explanation: Krishna describes existence as unmanifest before birth, manifest during life, and unmanifest after death. He then questions the basis for grief over this process.

source.sanskrit:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम्।

कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम्।।2.21।।
source.transliteration:
vedāvināśhinaṁ nityaṁ ya enam ajam avyayam
kathaṁ sa puruṣhaḥ pārtha kaṁ ghātayati hanti kam
source.translation: Whoever knows it to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and inexhaustible, how can that person slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain?

hook: Some truths can be heard many times and still remain difficult to understand.
simpleVersion: Krishna says the Self is seen, spoken about, and heard about with wonder, yet remains difficult for people to truly understand.
explanation: Krishna emphasizes how mysterious the Self is. People may encounter teachings about it with wonder, but genuine understanding remains rare.

source.sanskrit:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय

नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।

तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा

न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही।।2.22।।
source.transliteration:
vāsānsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya
navāni gṛihṇāti naro ’parāṇi
tathā śharīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇānya
nyāni sanyāti navāni dehī
source.translation: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so too the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the indwelling Self in every being is indestructible, so Arjuna should not grieve for any creature.
explanation: Krishna returns to His central point: the indwelling Self cannot be destroyed. On that basis, He tells Arjuna not to grieve for any being.

source.sanskrit:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः।

न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः।।2.23।।
source.transliteration:
nainaṁ chhindanti śhastrāṇi nainaṁ dahati pāvakaḥ
na chainaṁ kledayantyāpo na śhoṣhayati mārutaḥ
source.translation: Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the Self cannot be cut, burned, soaked, or dried; it is eternal and unchanging.
explanation: Krishna describes the Self as beyond every ordinary form of physical destruction. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, unmoving, and ancient.

source.sanskrit:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च।

नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः।।2.24।।
source.transliteration:
achchhedyo ’yam adāhyo ’yam akledyo ’śhoṣhya eva cha
nityaḥ sarva-gataḥ sthāṇur achalo ’yaṁ sanātanaḥ
source.translation: This Self cannot be cut, burned, wetted, nor dried up; it is eternal, all-pervasive, stable, immovable, and ancient.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the Self is unseen, beyond thought, and unchanging; knowing this, Arjuna should not grieve.
explanation: Krishna summarizes this part of His teaching by describing the Self as unmanifest, inconceivable, and unchanging, then tells Arjuna not to grieve.

source.sanskrit:
अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते।

तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि।।2.25।।
source.transliteration:
avyakto ’yam achintyo ’yam avikāryo ’yam uchyate
tasmādevaṁ viditvainaṁ nānuśhochitum arhasi
source.translation: This Self is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable, and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this to be so, you should not grieve.

simpleVersion: Even if Arjuna believed the Self is repeatedly born and dies, Krishna says grief would still not be justified.
explanation: Krishna offers this as an alternative argument: even under the belief that the Self is constantly born and dying, He says Arjuna should still not grieve.

source.sanskrit:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम्।

तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि।।2.26।।
source.transliteration:
atha chainaṁ nitya-jātaṁ nityaṁ vā manyase mṛitam
tathāpi tvaṁ mahā-bāho naivaṁ śhochitum arhasi
source.translation: But even if thou thinkest of It as constantly being born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, thou shouldst not grieve.

simpleVersion: Krishna says birth leads inevitably to death, and death leads to birth, so there is no escaping this cycle.
explanation: Krishna states that death is certain for whatever is born and birth is certain for whatever dies. He calls this unavoidable.

source.sanskrit:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च।

तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि।।2.27।।
source.transliteration:
jātasya hi dhruvo mṛityur dhruvaṁ janma mṛitasya cha
tasmād aparihārye ’rthe na tvaṁ śhochitum arhasi
source.translation: For the born, death is certain, and for the dead, birth is certain; therefore, you should not grieve over the inevitable.

simpleVersion: Krishna says beings are unmanifest before birth, visible during life, and unmanifest again after death.
explanation: Krishna describes the visible part of life as a middle stage between two unmanifest states. He then asks why this should be a cause for grief.

source.sanskrit:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत।

अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना।।2.28।।
source.transliteration:
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyakta-madhyāni bhārata
avyakta-nidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā
source.translation: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifest again in their end. What is there to grieve about?

hook: The deepest truths may be easy to hear but difficult to truly understand.
simpleVersion: Krishna says people encounter the Self with wonder, yet even after hearing about it, few truly understand it.
explanation: The verse emphasizes the mystery of the Self. Seeing, describing, or hearing about it does not automatically produce understanding.

source.sanskrit:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन

माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः।

आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः श्रृणोति

श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित्।।2.29।।
source.transliteration:
āśhcharya-vat paśhyati kaśhchid enan
āśhcharya-vad vadati tathaiva chānyaḥ
āśhcharya-vach chainam anyaḥ śhṛiṇoti
śhrutvāpyenaṁ veda na chaiva kaśhchit
source.translation: One sees this (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; yet, having heard, none understands it at all.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the indwelling Self in every being is indestructible, so Arjuna should not grieve.
explanation: Krishna closes this section by repeating that the Self within every being cannot be destroyed. Therefore, He tells Arjuna not to grieve.

source.sanskrit:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत।

तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि।।2.30।।
source.transliteration:
dehī nityam avadhyo ’yaṁ dehe sarvasya bhārata
tasmāt sarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṁ śhochitum arhasi
source.translation: This indweller in the body of everyone is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, you should not grieve for any creature.

hook: Your duty matters too.
simpleVersion: Krishna shifts from the nature of the Self to Arjuna's duty as a warrior and says he should not abandon a righteous battle.
explanation: Krishna now gives Arjuna a different reason to act. Beyond the question of life and death, Arjuna has a duty connected to his role as a warrior, and Krishna tells him not to waver from it.

source.sanskrit:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि।

धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाछ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते।।2.31।।
source.transliteration:
swa-dharmam api chāvekṣhya na vikampitum arhasi
dharmyāddhi yuddhāch chhreyo ’nyat kṣhatriyasya na vidyate
source.translation: Further, having regard to your duty, you should not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.

simpleVersion: Krishna describes a righteous battle as a rare opportunity for a warrior and compares it to an open door to heaven.
explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that warriors are fortunate when such a battle arises naturally and is considered righteous. He describes it as an open door to heaven.

source.sanskrit:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम्।

सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम्।।2.32।।
source.transliteration:
yadṛichchhayā chopapannaṁ swarga-dvāram apāvṛitam
sukhinaḥ kṣhatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddham īdṛiśham
source.translation: Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called to fight in such a battle that comes of its own accord as an open door to heaven.

hook: What happens when avoiding your duty becomes a choice with consequences?
simpleVersion: Krishna warns that refusing this righteous battle would mean abandoning Arjuna's duty and reputation and incurring sin.
explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that refusing to fight would mean giving up his prescribed duty and reputation, with serious moral consequences according to Krishna's teaching.

source.sanskrit:
अथ चैत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि।

ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि।।2.33।।
source.transliteration:
atha chet tvam imaṁ dharmyaṁ saṅgrāmaṁ na kariṣhyasi
tataḥ sva-dharmaṁ kīrtiṁ cha hitvā pāpam avāpsyasi
source.translation: But if you will not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned your own duty and reputation, you will incur sin.

simpleVersion: Krishna says that for someone who has been honored, lasting dishonor can be worse than death.
explanation: Krishna warns that people will speak of Arjuna's dishonor if he abandons the battle. He says such dishonor is especially painful for someone who has been respected.

source.sanskrit:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम्।

संभावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते।।2.34।।
source.transliteration:
akīrtiṁ chāpi bhūtāni
kathayiṣhyanti te ’vyayām
sambhāvitasya chākīrtir
maraṇād atirichyate
source.translation: People will also recount your everlasting dishonor; and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.

simpleVersion: Krishna says other great warriors may think Arjuna withdrew from fear and may lose their respect for him.
explanation: Krishna explains how Arjuna's withdrawal could be interpreted by other warriors. Those who once respected him might think he left the battle out of fear.

source.sanskrit:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः।

येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम्।।2.35।।
source.transliteration:
bhayād raṇād uparataṁ mansyante tvāṁ mahā-rathāḥ
yeṣhāṁ cha tvaṁ bahu-mato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam
source.translation: The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear, and you will be held in low esteem by those who have held you in high regard.

simpleVersion: Krishna says Arjuna's enemies would mock his strength and speak insulting words about him.
explanation: Krishna warns that Arjuna's enemies would use his withdrawal as an opportunity to insult his abilities. He asks what could be more painful than such abuse.

source.sanskrit:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून् वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः।

निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम्।।2.36।।
source.transliteration:
avāchya-vādānśh cha bahūn vadiṣhyanti tavāhitāḥ
nindantastava sāmarthyaṁ tato duḥkhataraṁ nu kim
source.translation: Your enemies, scoffing at your power, will speak many abusive words—what could be more painful than this?

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to rise and fight with determination, saying victory brings earthly enjoyment and death brings heaven.
explanation: Krishna presents two possible outcomes of the battle and urges Arjuna to stand up with a firm decision to fight.

source.sanskrit:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम्।

तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः।।2.37।।
source.transliteration:
hato vā prāpsyasi swargaṁ jitvā vā bhokṣhyase mahīm
tasmād uttiṣhṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛita-niśhchayaḥ
source.translation: Slain, you will obtain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.

hook: Can you act steadily without letting success or failure decide your state of mind?
simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike and act from duty.
explanation: Krishna introduces equanimity as the basis for action. He tells Arjuna to remain balanced through opposite outcomes and perform his duty without attachment to them.

source.sanskrit:
सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ।

ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि।।2.38।।
source.transliteration:
sukha-duḥkhe same kṛitvā lābhālābhau jayājayau
tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṁ pāpam avāpsyasi
source.translation: Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat equal, engage in battle for the sake of battle; thus, you shall not incur sin.

simpleVersion: Krishna says He has explained the path of knowledge and will now explain the wisdom of Yoga that frees action from bondage.
explanation: Krishna marks a transition in His teaching, moving from the philosophical discussion of knowledge to the practical wisdom of Yoga and action.

source.sanskrit:
एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां श्रृणु।

बुद्ध्यायुक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि।।2.39।।
source.transliteration:
eṣhā te ’bhihitā sānkhye
buddhir yoge tvimāṁ śhṛiṇu
buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha
karma-bandhaṁ prahāsyasi
source.translation: This, which has been taught to you, is wisdom concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, you shall cast off the bonds of action.

hook: No sincere step on this path is wasted.
simpleVersion: Krishna says no effort on this path is lost, and even a small amount of this practice can protect a person from great fear.
explanation: Krishna reassures Arjuna that sincere progress on this path has lasting value. Even a small amount of this practice is described as protection from great fear.

source.sanskrit:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते।

स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात्।।2.40।।
source.transliteration:
nehābhikrama-nāśho ’sti pratyavāyo na vidyate
svalpam apyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt
source.translation: In this, there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm produced, nor any transgression. Even a little of this knowledge protects one from great fear.

hook: A scattered mind pulls in many directions; a steady mind knows where it is going.
simpleVersion: Krishna contrasts one-pointed determination with the endless branching thoughts of an indecisive mind.
explanation: The verse contrasts focused determination with indecision. A steady mind has one clear direction, while an undecided mind becomes scattered among many competing aims.

source.sanskrit:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन।

बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम्।।2.41।।
source.transliteration:
vyavasāyātmikā buddhir ekeha kuru-nandana
bahu-śhākhā hyanantāśh cha buddhayo ’vyavasāyinām
source.translation: Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is only one single-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the indecisive.

simpleVersion: Krishna criticizes people who become absorbed in elaborate scriptural promises and say there is nothing beyond them.
explanation: Krishna describes people He considers unwise who delight in flowery religious language and insist that the promises described there are the whole of spiritual life.

source.sanskrit:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः।

वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः।।2.42।।
source.transliteration:
yāmimāṁ puṣhpitāṁ vāchaṁ pravadanty-avipaśhchitaḥ
veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha nānyad astīti vādinaḥ
source.translation: The unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogizing words of the Vedas, utter flowery speech, saying, "There is nothing else," O Arjuna.

simpleVersion: Krishna says such people are driven by desire for pleasure, power, and heavenly rewards and become absorbed in elaborate rituals.
explanation: Krishna continues describing a desire-driven approach to religion: seeking heavenly rewards, pleasure, and power through many prescribed actions.

source.sanskrit:
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम्।

क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति।।2.43।।
source.transliteration:
kāmātmānaḥ svarga-parā 

 janma-karma-phala-pradām

 kriyā-viśeṣa-bahulāṁ

 bhogaiśvarya-gatiṁ prati
source.translation: Full of desires, with heaven as their goal, (they speak words that are directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods abounding in specific actions, for the attainment of pleasure and power.

hook: When pleasure and power become the main goal, where does inner steadiness go?
simpleVersion: Krishna says attachment to pleasure and power prevents the focused understanding needed for steady meditation.
explanation: Krishna explains that a mind heavily attached to pleasure and power loses the one-pointed steadiness needed for meditation and inner realization.

source.sanskrit:
भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम्।

व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते।।2.44।।
source.transliteration:
bhogaiśwvarya-prasaktānāṁ tayāpahṛita-chetasām
vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate
source.translation: For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teachings, their determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and Samadhi (superconscious state).

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to rise above the three qualities, remain balanced, and become established in the Self.
explanation: Krishna instructs Arjuna to move beyond the three qualities discussed in the teaching, remain free from opposites, and stay grounded in the Self rather than constant acquisition and preservation.

source.sanskrit:
त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन।

निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान्।।2.45।।
source.transliteration:
trai-guṇya-viṣhayā vedā nistrai-guṇyo bhavārjuna
nirdvandvo nitya-sattva-stho niryoga-kṣhema ātmavān
source.translation: The Vedas deal with the three attributes; be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites and ever remain in the quality of Sattva, freed from acquisition and preservation, and be established in the Self.

simpleVersion: Krishna compares the value of scripture to a small reservoir during a flood for someone who has realized the Self.
explanation: Krishna uses the flood-and-reservoir image to explain that for one who has directly realized the Self, the limited function served by scripture has already been surpassed.

source.sanskrit:
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके।

तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः।।2.46।।
source.transliteration:
yāvān artha udapāne sarvataḥ samplutodake
tāvānsarveṣhu vedeṣhu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ
source.translation: To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as a reservoir of water would be in a place where there is a flood.

hook: You can control your effort; you cannot command the result.
simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to focus on action rather than claiming its results, without using detachment as an excuse for inaction.
explanation: Krishna gives Arjuna responsibility for performing his work, not for controlling or claiming its outcome. He also warns against both result-driven action and avoiding action altogether.
lifeLesson: Do your part sincerely without making the outcome the measure of your worth.

source.sanskrit:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।

मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि।।2.47।।
source.transliteration:
karmaṇy-evādhikāras te mā phaleṣhu kadāchana
mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo ’stvakarmaṇi
source.translation: Your right is only to work, but not to its results; do not let the results of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.

hook: What if success and failure stopped deciding your inner state?
simpleVersion: Krishna defines Yoga as acting without attachment while remaining balanced in success and failure.
explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to act while giving up attachment to outcomes. He describes this evenness of mind in success and failure as Yoga.

source.sanskrit:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।

सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते।।2.48।।
source.transliteration:
yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya
siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga uchyate
source.translation: Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure; evenness of mind is called Yoga.

simpleVersion: Krishna says acting with steady wisdom is higher than action driven by results, and urges Arjuna to seek refuge in wisdom.
explanation: Krishna places wisdom above result-driven action. He tells Arjuna to ground himself in that wisdom rather than making the fruits of action his motive.

source.sanskrit:
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनञ्जय।

बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः।।2.49।।
source.transliteration:
dūreṇa hy-avaraṁ karma buddhi-yogād dhanañjaya
buddhau śharaṇam anvichchha kṛipaṇāḥ phala-hetavaḥ
source.translation: Far lower than the Yoga of wisdom is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are those whose motive is the fruit.

hook: Yoga is not just doing more; it is learning how to act wisely.
simpleVersion: Krishna says a person established in wisdom moves beyond being bound by good and bad results, calling Yoga skill in action.
explanation: Krishna connects wisdom with skillful action. Acting with steadiness changes the way a person relates to the consequences of what they do.

source.sanskrit:
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते।

तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम्।।2.50।।
source.transliteration:
buddhi-yukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛita-duṣhkṛite
tasmād yogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśhalam
source.translation: Endowed with wisdom and evenness of mind, one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote yourself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the wise give up attachment to the fruits of action and become free from the bonds of repeated birth.
explanation: Krishna describes the result of acting with wisdom: freedom from attachment to results and, ultimately, freedom from the cycle of birth described in the verse.

source.sanskrit:
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः।

जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम्।।2.51।।
source.transliteration:
karma-jaṁ buddhi-yuktā hi phalaṁ tyaktvā manīṣhiṇaḥ
janma-bandha-vinirmuktāḥ padaṁ gachchhanty-anāmayam
source.translation: The wise, possessing knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the bonds of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil.

simpleVersion: Krishna says that when Arjuna's understanding rises beyond confusion, he will become free from being pulled by what he has heard or still needs to hear.
explanation: Krishna says that clearer understanding brings freedom from the confusion created by competing things one has heard or expects to hear.

source.sanskrit:
यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति।

तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च।।2.52।।
source.transliteration:
yadā te moha-kalilaṁ buddhir vyatitariṣhyati
tadā gantāsi nirvedaṁ śhrotavyasya śhrutasya cha
source.translation: When your intellect passes beyond the mire of delusion, then you will attain indifference to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard.

hook: When the mind becomes steady, confusion loses its grip.
simpleVersion: Krishna says that when Arjuna's understanding becomes steady and unwavering, he will attain Yoga.
explanation: Krishna describes a mind that is no longer pulled around by conflicting teachings. When the intellect becomes steady in deep concentration, Yoga is attained.

source.sanskrit:
श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला।

समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि।।2.53।।
source.transliteration:
śhruti-vipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niśhchalā
samādhāv-achalā buddhis tadā yogam avāpsyasi
source.translation: When your intellect, which is perplexed by the Vedic texts you have read, stands immovable and steady in the Self, then you will attain Self-realization.

hook: What does real inner steadiness look like in everyday life?
simpleVersion: Arjuna asks Krishna how a person of steady wisdom speaks, sits, and moves through the world.
explanation: Arjuna now wants a practical description of the person Krishna has been discussing. He asks how such a person behaves in ordinary life.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव।

स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम्।।2.54।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
sthita-prajñasya kā bhāṣhā samādhi-sthasya keśhava
sthita-dhīḥ kiṁ prabhāṣheta kim āsīta vrajeta kim
source.translation: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, what is the description of one who has steady wisdom and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how do they sit, and how do they walk?"

hook: What if contentment came from within instead of from getting what you want?
simpleVersion: Krishna says a person of steady wisdom gives up mental desires and finds satisfaction in the Self.
explanation: Krishna begins describing steady wisdom by saying that such a person lets go of desires arising in the mind and finds contentment in the Self.

source.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

प्रजहाति यदा कामान् सर्वान् पार्थ मनोगतान्।

आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते।।2.55।।
source.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha mano-gatān
ātmany-evātmanā tuṣhṭaḥ sthita-prajñas tadochyate
source.translation: The Blessed Lord said, "When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then he is said to be one of steady wisdom."

simpleVersion: Krishna describes steady wisdom as remaining calm in suffering, free from craving in pleasure, and beyond attachment, fear, and anger.
explanation: Krishna lists qualities of the steady sage: difficulty does not shake the mind, pleasure does not create craving, and attachment, fear, and anger no longer dominate.

source.sanskrit:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः।

वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते।।2.56।।
source.transliteration:
duḥkheṣhv-anudvigna-manāḥ sukheṣhu vigata-spṛihaḥ
vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ sthita-dhīr munir uchyate
source.translation: He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not long for pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.

simpleVersion: Krishna says steady wisdom means remaining unattached and neither clinging to good fortune nor resisting bad fortune.
explanation: Krishna describes emotional balance in changing circumstances. A person of steady wisdom does not become carried away by favorable events or hostile toward unfavorable ones.

source.sanskrit:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम्।

नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.57।।
source.transliteration:
yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehas tat tat prāpya śhubhāśhubham
nābhinandati na dveṣhṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: He who is everywhere without attachment, upon encountering anything good or bad, neither rejoices nor hastens; his wisdom is firm.

hook: A steady mind knows when to pull back.
simpleVersion: Krishna compares a disciplined person to a tortoise that withdraws its limbs, showing how the wise withdraw the senses from their objects.
explanation: The tortoise image illustrates deliberate sense control. The person with steady wisdom can withdraw attention from external objects instead of being constantly pulled toward them.

source.sanskrit:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः।

इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.58।।
source.transliteration:
yadā sanharate chāyaṁ kūrmo ’ṅgānīva sarvaśhaḥ
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyas tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: When, like the tortoise which withdraws all its limbs on all sides, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady.

hook: Avoiding temptation is not the same as outgrowing the desire for it.
simpleVersion: Krishna says that simply staying away from sense objects can leave the underlying craving behind; that craving fades through a higher realization.
explanation: The verse makes an important distinction: external restraint can remove contact with an object while leaving the inner taste for it. Krishna says that deeper realization is what removes that longing.

source.sanskrit:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः।

रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते।।2.59।।
source.transliteration:
viṣhayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ
rasa-varjaṁ raso ’pyasya paraṁ dṛiṣhṭvā nivartate
source.translation: The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man, leaving the longing behind; but his longing also turns away upon seeing the Supreme.

hook: Even a disciplined mind can be pulled away by the senses.
simpleVersion: Krishna warns that powerful senses can drag away the mind even when a wise person is trying to control them.
explanation: Krishna acknowledges that sense control is difficult. Even someone striving for wisdom can have the mind forcefully carried away by the senses.

source.sanskrit:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः।

इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः।।2.60।।
source.transliteration:
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣhasya vipaśhchitaḥ
indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṁ manaḥ
source.translation: The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, can violently carry away the mind of a wise person, even though they are striving to control them.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to restrain the senses and keep the mind focused on Him, because mastery of the senses supports steady wisdom.
explanation: Krishna gives the response to the previous danger: restrain the senses and remain devoted to Him. He connects mastery of the senses with steady wisdom.

source.sanskrit:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः।

वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.61।।
source.transliteration:
tāni sarvāṇi sanyamya yukta āsīta mat-paraḥ
vaśhe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: Having restrained them all, he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control.

hook: What you repeatedly think about can quietly become what you crave.
simpleVersion: Krishna describes a chain in which dwelling on an object creates attachment, attachment creates desire, and desire creates anger.
explanation: Krishna shows how a reaction can begin before anger appears. Repeated attention creates attachment, attachment creates desire, and blocked desire gives rise to anger.

source.sanskrit:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।

सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते।।2.62।।
source.transliteration:
dhyāyato viṣhayān puṁsaḥ saṅgas teṣhūpajāyate
saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho ’bhijāyate
source.translation: When one thinks of objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger arises.

hook: Anger can begin a chain that ends with the loss of clear judgment.
simpleVersion: Krishna says anger leads to confusion, confusion disrupts memory, and the loss of judgment leads to ruin.
explanation: Krishna continues the chain from the previous verse. Anger clouds understanding, that confusion affects memory, and damaged judgment can ultimately destroy a person's ability to act wisely.

source.sanskrit:
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः।

स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति।।2.63।।
source.transliteration:
krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ sammohāt smṛiti-vibhramaḥ
smṛiti-bhranśhād buddhi-nāśho buddhi-nāśhāt praṇaśhyati
source.translation: Anger leads to delusion, which causes loss of memory; this, in turn, leads to the destruction of discrimination, resulting in destruction.

hook: Peace begins when attraction and aversion stop controlling you.
simpleVersion: Krishna says a self-controlled person can move among sense objects without being ruled by attraction or aversion and thereby attain peace.
